sections.b: Abram's story begins with a command and a promise: "Go ... to the land I will show you," and "All the clans of the earth will find blessing in you" (Genesis 12:1–3). He leaves Haran at 75, travels through Canaan building altars, and goes down to Egypt in a famine, where he passes off his wife as his sister (12:10–20). He gives Lot the first choice of land (13:8–11), rescues him from four kings and is blessed by Melchizedek (14). God makes a covenant with him in a vision (15), renames him Abraham, "father of a multitude," and gives circumcision as a sign (17).
sections.refs: Genesis 12:1–9; Genesis 12:10–20; Genesis 13:8–18; Genesis 14:13–24; Genesis 15:1–21; Genesis 17:1–14

sections.b: Abraham welcomes three visitors and bargains with God for Sodom (18), fails again at Gerar (20), sends away Hagar and Ishmael (21) and, at the height of the story, is told to offer Isaac (22). He buys a grave for Sarah (23), sends for a wife for Isaac (24) and dies "old and satisfied" (25:8). Scripture calls him God's friend (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23). The story does not hide his fear and his failures; it shows a faith that grows through them.
sections.refs: Genesis 18:1–33; Genesis 20:1–18; Genesis 21:8–21; Genesis 22:1–19; Genesis 25:7–10; Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23

sections.b: For Jews, Abraham is Avraham avinu, "our father," the first to know the one God and the model of kindness; the Mishnah counts ten trials that he withstood (Avot 5:3). For Christians, he is the father of all who believe, justified by faith before circumcision (Romans 4; Galatians 3), and his offering of Isaac foreshadows the cross (Hebrews 11:17–19). For Muslims, Ibrahim is a hanif, a pure monotheist who was "neither Jew nor Christian" (Qur'an 3:67), who broke his people's idols, and who with Ishmael built the Kaaba at Mecca (Qur'an 2:125–129). All three tell the story of his turning from idols, which Genesis does not tell but Joshua 24:2 hints at.

common: Abraham is the shared ancestor in faith of Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
God's promise to bless all nations through Abraham (Genesis 12:3) frames the whole Bible's story.
uncommon: Some scholars think Abraham was originally a hero of Hebron and the south, joined to the Jacob traditions of the north only later.

claude.title: A flawed man of faith
claude.body: What strikes me most is how honestly Genesis draws Abraham. He trusts God enough to leave everything, then twice gives away his wife to save himself. He believes the promise, then takes Hagar to hurry it along. The story seems less interested in a model saint than in a God who keeps a promise through a man who is learning to trust it.

sections.b: Sarai is introduced as barren (Genesis 11:30). Twice she is passed off as Abraham's sister and taken by a king (12:10–20; 20:1–18). She gives Hagar to Abraham and then drives her away (16; 21). God renames her Sarah, "princess," and promises she will be "nations" (17:15–16). When she overhears that she will bear a son, she laughs to herself, and God asks, "Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?" (18:12–14). She names her son Isaac, "he laughs," and says, "God has made laughter for me" (21:6). Her death and burial at Hebron make her grave the family's first land in Canaan (23).
sections.refs: Genesis 11:30; Genesis 16:1–6; Genesis 17:15–21; Genesis 18:9–15; Genesis 21:1–7; Genesis 23:1–20

sections.b: Isaiah 51:2 calls exiles to look to Abraham and Sarah. Hebrews 11:11 honors her faith, on the traditional reading (many scholars take the verse as speaking of Abraham, with Sarah named as barren); 1 Peter 3:6 praises her respect for her husband; Paul uses her, the free woman, as a figure of the new covenant (Galatians 4:21–31). The rabbis counted her among the seven prophetesses (Megillah 14a) and said she was a greater prophet than Abraham, since God told him, "Whatever Sarah tells you, listen to her" (Genesis 21:12; Rashi).

common: Sarah is the mother of the promise: the covenant line passes through her son, not Hagar's.
uncommon: Some feminist readers see Sarah as a woman whose survival in a male world led her to oppress the one woman below her.

sections.b: Hagar is an Egyptian slave given to Abraham by Sarah to bear a child (Genesis 16:1–3). When she conceives and Sarah mistreats her, she runs away. The angel of the LORD finds her at a spring, sends her back, and promises her countless offspring and a son named Ishmael, "God hears" (16:7–12). She names God El Roi, "God who sees" (16:13). Years later she and her son are sent away; when the water runs out, God hears the boy and shows her a well (21:14–19). She is the first person in the Bible to be visited by the angel of the LORD.

Paul makes Hagar a figure of Sinai and slavery, set against Sarah the free woman (Galatians 4:21–31). Some rabbis said she was Pharaoh's daughter and later identified her with Keturah (Genesis Rabbah 45:1; 61:4). In Islam, Hajar is the faithful mother of Ishmael whom Abraham left in the valley of Mecca; her search for water between the hills of Safa and Marwa is re-enacted by every pilgrim, and the well of Zamzam is the spring God gave her (Bukhari). Womanist theologians such as Delores Williams have made her a figure of Black women's survival.

common: Hagar's story shows God caring for the outsider and the oppressed, even outside the covenant line.
uncommon: Some read Galatians 4 as Paul's argument about two covenants rather than a judgment on Hagar herself.

sections.b: Ishmael is Abraham's firstborn, by Hagar (Genesis 16:15). Before his birth he is called "a wild donkey of a man" who will live "in the face of all his brothers" (16:12). God promises to bless him and make him a great nation with twelve princes, but the covenant goes to Isaac (17:18–21). At Isaac's weaning he is seen "laughing" or "playing," and Sarah has him sent away (21:9–10); God hears him in the desert and is "with the boy" (21:17–20). He and Isaac bury Abraham together (25:9), and his twelve sons become tribes of Arabia (25:12–18).

In the Qur'an, Ismail is a prophet, "true to his promise" (Qur'an 19:54), who helped his father build the Kaaba (2:127). Most Muslim scholars hold that he, not Isaac, was the son Abraham was asked to sacrifice (37:99–113), though some early authorities named Isaac. Islamic genealogy traces Muhammad to him. Jewish tradition is mixed: the rabbis said he mocked Isaac or worshiped idols, but also that he repented before Abraham's death (Bava Batra 16b).

common: Ishmael is blessed by God and made a great nation, even though the covenant passes through Isaac.
uncommon: Some modern Jewish and Christian readers see the promise to Ishmael as grounds for a positive theology of Islam.

sections.b: Isaac is promised to Abraham and Sarah when both laugh at the thought (Genesis 17:17–19; 18:12–15), and his name means "he laughs." His birth at last, when Abraham is a hundred, fulfills the promise (21:1–7). He is weaned with a feast, and Ishmael is sent away so that he alone will inherit (21:8–12). Paul calls believers "like Isaac, children of the promise" (Galatians 4:28).

Abraham's servant goes to Mesopotamia and, guided by prayer at a well, finds Rebekah (Genesis 24). Isaac meets her in the field at evening and loves her, "Isaac was comforted after his mother" (24:63–67). He prays for her when she is barren, and she bears twins (25:21–26).

common: Isaac is the child of promise, born when his parents had given up hope.

sections.b: God tells Abraham to offer "your son, your only one, whom you love, Isaac" on a mountain in Moriah (Genesis 22:2). Abraham obeys; at the last moment the angel stops him and a ram is offered instead. Judaism calls this the Akedah, "binding," and reads it at the New Year; the Midrash says Isaac was a grown man who consented. Christians from Hebrews (11:17–19) and the early fathers on read it as a figure of God giving his Son. Islam tells the story of Abraham's son, usually taken as Ishmael (Qur'an 37:102–107). Kierkegaard asked whether such obedience could be ethical; many modern readers see the story as a rejection of child sacrifice.

common: The Akedah is the supreme test of Abraham's faith and a central text for Jews, Christians and Muslims.
uncommon: A medieval Jewish tradition, voiced in some midrash and poems, imagined that Isaac was actually sacrificed and raised again.

claude.title: Reading the hardest chapter
claude.body: Genesis 22 is told with almost no feeling stated at all, and that silence does much of the work. I think it is fair to read it both as a story of radical trust and as one that says something about child sacrifice, since the God who asks for Isaac also stops the knife. What I would not do is make it easy: every tradition that loves this story has also argued with it.

sections.b: Lot travels with his uncle Abram from Haran (Genesis 12:4). When their herds grow too large, Abram lets him choose, and Lot picks the well-watered plain of the Jordan and moves toward Sodom (13:10–13). Captured by four kings, he is rescued by Abram (14:12–16). Two angels come to Sodom; Lot takes them in and offers his daughters to the mob, a scene many readers find shocking (19:1–11). The angels drag him out; his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt (19:26). In a cave his daughters make him drunk and conceive Moab and Ammon (19:30–38).

Jesus uses the days of Lot as a picture of sudden judgment and warns, "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:28–32). 2 Peter 2:7–8 calls Lot "righteous," tormented by the lawlessness around him, though Genesis gives a more mixed picture. Wisdom 10:6 says Wisdom rescued him. The Qur'an counts Lut among the prophets, who warned his people and was saved with his family except his wife (Qur'an 11:77–83).

common: Lot is a cautionary figure: a man who drifted toward Sodom and was saved, as Genesis says, because God remembered Abraham (19:29).
uncommon: Some feminist readers focus on Lot's daughters as victims twice over, first offered to the mob and then left to survive alone.

sections.b: After Abram rescues Lot, Melchizedek, "king of Salem" and "priest of God Most High," brings out bread and wine and blesses him; Abram gives him a tenth of everything (Genesis 14:18–20). His name means "my king is righteousness." Salem is identified with Jerusalem in Psalm 76:2. He appears from nowhere and vanishes, with no family or death recorded.

Psalm 110:4 promises the king, "You are a priest forever, after the pattern of Melchizedek." Hebrews 5–7 builds on both texts: Jesus is a priest not by descent from Levi but in Melchizedek's order, a priesthood older than Levi's, since Levi "paid tithes in Abraham" (Hebrews 7:9–10). A Dead Sea Scroll (11Q13) makes Melchizedek a heavenly deliverer. The Talmud and Targums identify him with Shem (Nedarim 32b). Christian tradition linked his bread and wine with the Eucharist (Cyprian).

common: Hebrews reads Melchizedek as a type of Christ, the eternal priest-king.
uncommon: Some scholars think the Melchizedek scene was added to give David's Jerusalem an ancient link to Abraham.

sections.b: God makes his covenant with Abram twice. In Genesis 15, Abram cuts animals in two and a smoking oven and flaming torch pass between the pieces: God binds himself by oath to give the land "from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates" (15:17–21). In Genesis 17, God gives the covenant of circumcision, renames Abram and Sarai, and promises to be God to Abraham's offspring "a covenant that lasts forever" (17:7). Many scholars compare chapter 15 to royal land grants of the ancient Near East (Weinfeld), in which a king rewards a loyal servant.

Critical scholars usually assign chapter 15 to J or E and chapter 17 to P, two tellings of one covenant. Traditional readers see one covenant in stages: promised in 12, sealed by oath in 15, given its sign in 17 and confirmed by oath after the Akedah (22:16–18). Paul stresses that the promise came 430 years before the Law and so cannot be set aside by it (Galatians 3:17).

God commands Abraham to circumcise every male, including slaves, on the eighth day, as "the sign of the covenant" (Genesis 17:10–14). Abraham, at 99, and Ishmael, at 13, are circumcised the same day (17:23–26); Isaac is circumcised on the eighth day (21:4). Egyptians and other neighbors also circumcised, often at puberty; Genesis gives the old practice a new meaning and moves it to infancy. Jews still hold the brit milah on the eighth day; Muslims practice circumcision as part of the way of Abraham, often citing Ishmael's age at circumcision.

"Abram put his trust in the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). The verb (he'emin) means to rely on, to consider firm. Paul argues that Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, so he is the father of all who believe (Romans 4:1–12; Galatians 3:6–9). James quotes the same verse but stresses that Abraham's faith was completed by works when he offered Isaac (James 2:21–23). Jewish tradition reads 15:6 alongside Abraham's faithfulness in trials (1 Maccabees 2:52) and the Mekhilta says Abraham inherited this world and the world to come by faith, citing 15:6. Hebrews 11 makes Abraham's journey, his waiting and his offering of Isaac the longest example in its list.

The Septuagint made 15:6 passive, "it was reckoned to him," and Paul and James both quote that form. Paul stresses that 15:6 comes before the circumcision of chapter 17 (Romans 4:9–12). James reads it with chapter 22 and concludes that "a person is made right by works and not by faith alone" (James 2:24). Luther and Calvin read Paul as teaching justification by faith alone. The Council of Trent (Session 6, 1547) rejected "faith alone" if it meant faith without hope and love, while also teaching that no one earns the grace of justification. The New Perspective on Paul (E. P. Sanders, James Dunn, N. T. Wright) reads the "works of the Law" Paul rejects mainly as the markers that set Jews apart, so that Romans 4 is about Gentiles joining Abraham's family. In 1999 Lutherans and Catholics signed the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, agreeing that a person is accepted by God by grace alone, through faith, and not because of any merit, while keeping some differences.
sections.refs: Genesis 15:6; Genesis 22:1–19; Romans 3:28; Romans 4:9–12; Galatians 2:16; James 2:21–24

common: Genesis 15:6 is the classic proof text for justification by faith in Protestant theology.
uncommon: Some interpreters read 15:6 as Abram counting God righteous, not God counting Abram righteous; the Hebrew allows either subject.

claude.title: Paul and James are not far apart
claude.body: Paul and James use the same verse for what looks like opposite points. I read them as answering different questions: Paul asks what puts a person right with God in the first place, and James asks what real faith looks like when it is tested. Genesis gives both, with 15:6 and chapter 22 standing seven chapters apart.

sections.b: God promises the land to Abram's offspring as soon as he arrives (Genesis 12:7) and tells him to look in every direction and walk its length (13:14–17). The borders are drawn "from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates," the land of ten peoples (15:18–21). Yet Abraham calls himself "a foreigner living among you as a settler" (23:4), and the only land he ever owns is a grave (23:17–20). Stephen notes that God "gave him no share of it to inherit, not even room to plant a foot" (Acts 7:5). Hebrews says the patriarchs died in faith, seeking "a better homeland, a heavenly one" (Hebrews 11:13–16).
sections.refs: Genesis 12:7; Genesis 13:14–17; Genesis 15:18–21; Genesis 17:8; Genesis 23:4; Acts 7:5; Hebrews 11:9–16

common: The gap between promise and possession runs through the Abraham story and the whole Pentateuch.
uncommon: Some scholars see the wide Euphrates borders as reflecting the ideal of Solomon's day (1 Kings 4:21) rather than any real holding.

sections.b: Adding up the Bible's figures places Abraham about 2100–1900 BC, and earlier conservative scholars, notably Albright and Speiser, saw the patriarchs as fitting the Middle Bronze Age: Amorite names like Abram and Jacob, wanderings between cities, and customs paralleled at Nuzi and Mari. From the 1970s Thomas L. Thompson and John Van Seters argued that the parallels fit the first millennium as well or better. Today many critical scholars see the stories as shaped in the monarchy or exile; conservative scholars such as Kitchen argue that names, treaty forms and slave prices fit the early second millennium.

Genesis gives Abraham camels (12:16; 24:10) and has him deal with Philistines (21:32–34). Bone studies show domestic camels became common in the southern Levant only around 1000–900 BC (Sapir-Hen and Ben-Yosef, 2013), and the Philistines arrived about 1175 BC. Critical scholars read these as anachronisms, signs of a later writer. Conservative scholars answer that camels were known as rare luxuries earlier, and that "Philistines" may be an updated name for earlier Aegean settlers, as "Dan" updates Laish (14:14). Others add that Ur "of the Chaldeans" (11:31; 15:7) uses a name from after 1000 BC.
sections.refs: Genesis 12:16; Genesis 14:14; Genesis 15:7; Genesis 21:32–34; Genesis 24:10; Genesis 26:1

common: Most scholars agree that, whatever their origin, the stories were written down long after the events they describe.
uncommon: Some scholars think the patriarchs were tribal or clan figures, personified ancestors rather than individuals.

claude.title: What the evidence can and cannot show
claude.body: Archaeology cannot prove or disprove that a herdsman named Abraham lived; such people leave no trace. What it can test is the setting, and there the record is mixed: some details fit the early second millennium, others look like later updating. I think the fairest summary is that the stories carry old memories in a form shaped much later, and that people of good faith weigh those two parts differently.

sections.b: Genesis 12–25 has long been a showcase for source theory. Three times a patriarch passes off his wife as his sister (12:10–20; 20; 26:6–11); Hagar leaves twice (16; 21); the covenant is made twice (15; 17); and God is called "the LORD" in some stories and "God" in others. Classic source theory assigned chapter 17, the genealogies, the ages and the burial at Machpelah to P (the Priestly source), chapter 20 and much of 21–22 to E, and most of the rest to J. Many scholars now doubt a separate E, and some see the stories as growing in layers rather than as whole documents woven together.
sections.refs: Genesis 12:10–20; Genesis 15:1–21; Genesis 16:1–16; Genesis 17:1–27; Genesis 20:1–18; Genesis 21:8–21; Genesis 23:1–20

sections.b: Jewish and Christian tradition held that Moses wrote the Torah, and many conservative scholars still defend Mosaic authorship with later editing, such as place names updated in later times (14:14). They explain the repeated stories as real repeated events or as deliberate literary patterns, and the different names of God by context: Cassuto argued that "God" stresses the Creator and "the LORD" the covenant God. Literary critics such as Robert Alter read the doublets as intended "type-scenes."

common: Most critical scholars still use the labels J, E and P, even when they reject the classic four-document theory.
uncommon: Some scholars argue that the Abraham stories were first composed as a whole, with the doublets placed on purpose.

sections.b: Lot settles near Sodom, whose people are "evil, great sinners against the LORD" (Genesis 13:13). God tells Abraham of the outcry against the city, and Abraham bargains for it down to ten righteous people (18:16–33). Two angels find violence at Lot's door, as the men of the city demand to "know" the visitors (19:4–5). Fire and sulfur fall on the cities of the plain (19:24–25). The prophets name Sodom's sins as injustice, pride and neglect of the poor, and Ezekiel adds that they "did a detestable thing" (Isaiah 1:10; Ezekiel 16:49–50), a word Leviticus uses of sex between men (Leviticus 18:22). Jubilees and the Testament of Naphtali stress sexual sin, as do Jude 7 ("other flesh") and 2 Peter 2:7. Traditional Jewish, Christian and Muslim teaching has read the story as condemning same-sex acts; others, following Bailey and later writers, see the sin as gang rape and the violation of hospitality, and point to Jesus linking Sodom with towns that refuse his messengers (Matthew 10:14–15). Some archaeologists have linked the cities to Bab edh-Dhra or to Tall el-Hammam, whose 2021 airburst study has been sharply challenged.
sections.refs: Genesis 13:10–13; Genesis 18:16–33; Genesis 19:1–29; Isaiah 1:10; Ezekiel 16:49–50; Leviticus 18:22; Matthew 10:14–15; 2 Peter 2:6–8; Jude 7

sections.h: Abraham at Mamre and Lot at Sodom
sections.b: Abraham runs from his tent in the heat of the day, bows, and gives three strangers water, rest, bread, a calf and curds (Genesis 18:1–8). He does not know they are the LORD and two angels. Lot also takes in strangers and defends them (19:1–8), while the men of Sodom attack them; the two chapters are built as a contrast. The rabbis made Abraham the model of hakhnasat orchim, welcoming guests, and the Talmud says that welcoming guests is greater than receiving the presence of God, learning it from Abraham leaving the LORD to run to his visitors (Shabbat 127a); later tradition added that his tent was open on all four sides. Hebrews 13:2 recalls the scene: some "without realizing it, have had angels as guests." Rebekah's watering of a stranger's camels shows the same virtue (24:17–20).
sections.refs: Genesis 18:1–8; Genesis 19:1–11; Genesis 24:17–33; Judges 19:15–24; Hebrews 13:2; Matthew 25:35

common: Hospitality to strangers is one of the highest virtues in the Bible's world, and violating it a grave sin.

sections.h: Names of God in Abraham's story
sections.b: Abraham's story is rich in divine names. Melchizedek blesses him by El Elyon, "God Most High" (Genesis 14:19). God introduces himself as El Shaddai, often rendered "God Almighty" (17:1). Hagar names God El Roi, "God who sees" (16:13). Abraham calls on El Olam, "the everlasting God," at Beersheba (21:33), and names the mountain of the Akedah YHWH Yireh, "the LORD will see" or "provide" (22:14). Abraham also addresses God as "Lord GOD" (Adonai YHWH, 15:2, 8). Exodus 6:3 says the patriarchs knew God as El Shaddai, not by the name YHWH, which critical scholars take as a sign of different sources.
sections.refs: Genesis 14:18–22; Genesis 15:2; Genesis 16:13; Genesis 17:1; Genesis 21:33; Genesis 22:14; Exodus 6:3

sections.b: The first tithe in the Bible is Abram's gift to Melchizedek of "a tenth of everything" from the spoils of war (Genesis 14:20). It is voluntary and given to a priest outside Israel. Hebrews argues that since Levi was still "in Abraham's body," the Levitical priesthood itself paid tithes to Melchizedek (Hebrews 7:4–10). Jacob later vows a tenth at Bethel (28:22).

Before Jacob and Esau are born, God tells Rebekah that "the elder will serve the younger" (Genesis 25:23). Paul uses this, with Malachi 1:2–3, to argue that God's purpose of election stands "not by works but by the one who calls" (Romans 9:10–13). The theme runs through Genesis: Isaac over Ishmael (21:12), Jacob over Esau, and later Ephraim over Manasseh. Calvinist readers see individual election to salvation; many others read the texts as God's choice of a people for a role in history.

Abraham calls himself "a foreigner living among you as a settler" when he speaks to the Hittites of Hebron (Genesis 23:4), and God tells him his offspring will be "foreigners in a land that is not theirs" (15:13). He lives at peace with outsiders: he allies with Amorites (14:13), receives a blessing from Melchizedek, makes a treaty with Abimelech (21:22–32) and is honored as "a prince of God" (23:6). Pharaoh and Abimelech, the foreign kings, often behave better than he does (12:18–20; 20:9–10). The Law reminds Israel to love the foreigner, "for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 10:19).
sections.refs: Genesis 14:13; Genesis 15:13; Genesis 20:9–11; Genesis 21:22–32; Genesis 23:4–6; Hebrews 11:9; 1 Peter 2:11

sections.b: The "angel of the LORD" first appears to Hagar (Genesis 16:7), and he speaks as God himself: "I will multiply and multiply your offspring" (16:10). Hagar then names the LORD who had spoken to her (16:13). At the Akedah the angel calls from heaven and says, "you have not held back your son, your only one, from me" (22:12). In Genesis 18 the LORD appears to Abraham as one of three men; two of them are called angels at Sodom (19:1). Jewish interpreters usually see the angel as God's messenger speaking in his name; many church fathers saw a pre-incarnate appearance of the Son (Justin).
sections.refs: Genesis 16:7–13; Genesis 18:1–2; Genesis 19:1; Genesis 21:17; Genesis 22:11–18; Exodus 3:2–6

sections.b: The word "bless" appears five times in God's first words to Abram (Genesis 12:2–3): God will bless him, make his name great, and make him a blessing, and "all the clans of the earth will find blessing in you." The verb in 12:3 and 18:18 is passive or middle in form; in 22:18 and 26:4 it is reflexive, "will bless themselves by your offspring," meaning the nations will use Abraham's name when they bless. The Septuagint and the New Testament read "will be blessed" (Acts 3:25; Galatians 3:8). Melchizedek blesses Abram (14:19), God blesses Abraham "in every way" (24:1), and after his death God blesses Isaac (25:11). Paul calls the gift of the Spirit to the Gentiles "the blessing of Abraham" (Galatians 3:14).
sections.refs: Genesis 12:2–3; Genesis 14:19–20; Genesis 18:18; Genesis 22:17–18; Genesis 24:1; Genesis 25:11; Acts 3:25; Galatians 3:8–14

common: Genesis 12:3 is read by Christians as the first announcement of the gospel to the nations (Galatians 3:8).
uncommon: Some scholars hold that all the verb forms in 12:3 mean only "will use your name in blessing," not "will receive blessing through you."

sections.h: Altars and offerings in Abraham's story
sections.b: Abraham builds altars wherever he settles (Genesis 12:7–8; 13:18) but offers no sacrifice until the covenant of the pieces, where he cuts a heifer, a goat, a ram and two birds (15:9–10). The great sacrifice of his story is the one that does not happen: God asks for Isaac as a burnt offering, and a ram is offered "in place of his son" (22:13). Israel's law later forbids child sacrifice outright (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31) and redeems every firstborn son (Exodus 13:13). Jews connect the ram with the shofar and with the later temple on Moriah; Christians see in the ram and in Isaac a figure of Christ; Muslims remember the ransom "with a great sacrifice" at Eid al-Adha.
sections.refs: Genesis 12:7–8; Genesis 15:9–10; Genesis 22:2; Genesis 22:13; Exodus 13:13; Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31

sections.b: Christian readers have found many types (patterns that point forward to Christ) in Genesis 12–25. Melchizedek, priest and king with no recorded beginning or end, is read as a type of Christ by Hebrews 7. The church fathers saw his bread and wine as a picture of the Eucharist (Cyprian). Isaac carrying the wood up the mountain was compared to Jesus carrying the cross (Melito of Sardis; Origen), and the ram caught in the thicket to Christ crowned with thorns. Paul reads Hagar and Sarah as two covenants, saying he speaks "allegorically" (Galatians 4:24). Jewish interpreters read the same stories as patterns for Israel's later history, for example the Akedah as the merit that protects Israel.

Abraham's household shows the strains of having more than one wife. Sarai gives Hagar to Abram as a wife so that she can "be built into a family through her" (Genesis 16:2–3), a custom known from Old Assyrian marriage contracts and the Laws of Hammurabi. Once Hagar conceives, rivalry follows, and both women suffer (16:4–6; 21:9–14). Later Abraham takes Keturah, and the sons of his "concubines" receive gifts but not the inheritance (25:1–6). Genesis does not condemn these marriages outright, but it tells them as stories of conflict, as it will with Jacob's wives.
